P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A bag has 6 red balls and 2 blue balls of the same size. Sana says, "The ball I pick will be red or blue, so P(red) =12= \dfrac{1}{2}=21​." The correct probability that a ball picked at random is red is:

count balls, not colours (Topic 2). Why it applies: each ball, not each colour, is equally likely.

Sana's answer: the two colours are not equally likely.
This is P(blue).
This is red balls ÷ blue balls — a ratio, and more than 1, so not a probability.
68=34\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}86​=43​.

Given: 6 red and 2 blue balls. Asked: P(red).

Concept used: count balls, not colours (Topic 2). Why it applies: each ball, not each colour, is equally likely.

  1. 1

    All outcomes: 6+2=86 + 2 = 86+2=8 balls.

  2. 2

    Favourable: 6 red. P(red)=68=34P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}P(red)=86​=43​.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Sana's answer: the two colours are not equally likely.
    • (b) ✘ This is P(blue).
    • (c) ✘ This is red balls ÷ blue balls — a ratio, and more than 1, so not a probability.
    • (d) ✔ 68=34\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}86​=43​.

  3. Check: P(blue)=28=14P(\text{blue}) = \dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4}P(blue)=82​=41​, and 34+14=1\dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = 143​+41​=1 ✔.

  4. Answer (d)

    Common trap: Giving each colour an equal share. There are three times as many red balls as blue ones.
P2● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Two dice are thrown together. The number of all possible outcomes is:

ordered pairs (first die, second die) (Topic 5). Why it applies: each of the 6 faces of the first die goes with each of the 6 faces of the second.

6×6=366 \times 6 = 366×6=36 ordered pairs.
6+66 + 66+6 — adding instead of multiplying.
This is the number of different sums (2 to 12), which are not the outcomes.
This is the number of outcomes for one die.

Given: two dice. Asked: the number of outcomes.

Concept used: ordered pairs (first die, second die) (Topic 5). Why it applies: each of the 6 faces of the first die goes with each of the 6 faces of the second.

  1. 1

    6×6=366 \times 6 = 366×6=36.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ 6×6=366 \times 6 = 366×6=36 ordered pairs.
    • (b) ✘ 6+66 + 66+6 — adding instead of multiplying.
    • (c) ✘ This is the number of different sums (2 to 12), which are not the outcomes.
    • (d) ✘ This is the number of outcomes for one die.

  2. Check: the first row of the grid alone, (1, 1) to (1, 6), already has 6 outcomes, and there are 6 rows ✔.

  3. Answer (a)

    Common trap: Choosing 11 because the sums go from 2 to 12.
P3● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

A whole number is chosen at random from 1 to 25. Find the probability that it is a prime number.

Full solution

Given: 25 equally likely numbers. Asked: P(prime).

Concept used: list the primes; 1 is not a prime (Topic 1). Why it applies: the favourable outcomes are the primes up to 25.

  1. 1

    All outcomes: 25.

  2. 2

    Primes: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 → 9.

  3. 3

    P(prime)=925P(\text{prime}) = \dfrac{9}{25}P(prime)=259​.

  4. Check: the numbers that are not prime: 1 and the 15 composites 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25 — that is 16, and 9+16=259 + 16 = 259+16=25 ✔.

  5. Answer 925\dfrac{9}{25}259​

    Common trap: Counting 1 as a prime gives 1025=25\dfrac{10}{25} = \dfrac{2}{5}2510​=52​.

P4● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards (face cards are kings, queens and jacks; aces are not face cards). The probability that it is a face card or an ace is:

aces are not face cards, so the two groups do not overlap (Topics 1, 4). Why it applies: "or" — add the two groups, taking away any overlap (here none).

This counts the face cards only.
This counts the aces only.
1652=413\dfrac{16}{52} = \dfrac{4}{13}5216​=134​.
This is the probability of "not an ace".

Given: 52 cards; 12 face cards; 4 aces. Asked: P(face card or ace).

Concept used: aces are not face cards, so the two groups do not overlap (Topics 1, 4). Why it applies: "or" — add the two groups, taking away any overlap (here none).

  1. 1

    Face cards 12 + aces 4 = 16.

  2. 2

    P=1652=413P = \dfrac{16}{52} = \dfrac{4}{13}P=5216​=134​.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ This counts the face cards only.
    • (b) ✘ This counts the aces only.
    • (c) ✔ 1652=413\dfrac{16}{52} = \dfrac{4}{13}5216​=134​.
    • (d) ✘ This is the probability of "not an ace".

  3. Check: the other cards are the 2s to 10s: 4×9=364 \times 9 = 364×9=36, and 16+36=5216 + 36 = 5216+36=52 ✔.

  4. Answer (c)

    Common trap: Taking the aces as face cards, then counting them twice: 16+452\dfrac{16 + 4}{52}5216+4​.
P5● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

A die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting (a) a number at least 3, (b) a number at most 3.

Full solution

Given: one die, faces 1 to 6. Asked: two probabilities.

Concept used: at least 3 = 3 or more; at most 3 = 3 or less (Topic 3). Why it applies: both include 3.

  1. 1

    (a) 3, 4, 5, 6 → 46=23\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}64​=32​.

  2. 2

    (b) 1, 2, 3 → 36=12\dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}63​=21​.

  3. Check: (a)'s complement is "less than 3" (1, 2): 26=13\dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}62​=31​, and 23+13=1\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} = 132​+31​=1 ✔.

  4. Answer (a) 23\dfrac{2}{3}32​ (b) 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​

    Common trap: Leaving out 3 in both parts: 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ and 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​.

P6● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that one die shows 1 and the other shows an even number.

Full solution

Given: 36 ordered pairs. Asked: P(one die 1, the other even).

Concept used: ordered pairs — (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different outcomes (Topic 5). Why it applies: "one die … the other" can be either die.

  1. 1

    All outcomes: 36.

  2. 2

    First die 1, second even: (1, 2), (1, 4), (1, 6). First die even, second 1: (2, 1), (4, 1), (6, 1). Favourable: 6.

  3. 3

    P=636=16P = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}P=366​=61​.

  4. Check: on the grid, these are 3 cells in row 1 and 3 cells in column 1, and no cell is in both (the corner (1, 1) is not even) ✔.

  5. Answer 16\dfrac{1}{6}61​

    Common trap: Listing only (1, 2), (1, 4), (1, 6) and answering 336=112\dfrac{3}{36} = \dfrac{1}{12}363​=121​.

P7● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

In a raffle, 75 tickets are sold and 15 of them win a prize. One ticket is chosen at random. Write the probability that it wins (a) as a fraction in lowest terms, (b) as a decimal, (c) as a percentage.

Full solution

Given: 75 tickets, 15 winners. Asked: P(win) in three forms.

Concept used: P=favourableallP = \dfrac{\text{favourable}}{\text{all}}P=allfavourable​; simplify; × 100% (Topics 1–2). Why it applies: each ticket is equally likely.

  1. 1

    (a) 1575=15\dfrac{15}{75} = \dfrac{1}{5}7515​=51​ (HCF 15).

  2. 2

    (b) 15=0.2\dfrac{1}{5} = 0.251​=0.2.

  3. 3

    (c) 0.2×100%=20%0.2 \times 100\% = 20\%0.2×100%=20%.

  4. Check: 20% of 75 tickets =0.2×75=15= 0.2 \times 75 = 15=0.2×75=15 ✔.

  5. Answer (a) 15\dfrac{1}{5}51​ (b) 0.2 (c) 20%

    Common trap: Writing the probability as 20 (forgetting the % sign) — a probability written as a number is never more than 1.

P8● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

The probability that a non-leap year chosen at random has 53 Mondays is:

365=52×7+1365 = 52 \times 7 + 1365=52×7+1 (Topic 4). Why it applies: only the 1 extra day can give a 53rd Monday.

This is for a leap year, which has 2 extra days.
The outcomes are the 7 possible extra days, not 365 days.
1 of the 7 equally likely extra days is a Monday.
There is no reason to divide by the 52 weeks.

Given: 365 days. Asked: P(53 Mondays).

Concept used: 365=52×7+1365 = 52 \times 7 + 1365=52×7+1 (Topic 4). Why it applies: only the 1 extra day can give a 53rd Monday.

  1. 1

    52 full weeks give 52 Mondays.

  2. 2

    The extra day is Monday in 1 case out of 7: P=17P = \dfrac{1}{7}P=71​.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ This is for a leap year, which has 2 extra days.
    • (b) ✘ The outcomes are the 7 possible extra days, not 365 days.
    • (c) ✔ 1 of the 7 equally likely extra days is a Monday.
    • (d) ✘ There is no reason to divide by the 52 weeks.

  3. Check: each of the 7 days has the same chance 17\dfrac{1}{7}71​ of being the extra day, and 7×17=17 \times \dfrac{1}{7} = 17×71​=1 ✔.

  4. Answer (c)

    Common trap: Mixing up the ordinary year (17\dfrac{1}{7}71​) and the leap year (27\dfrac{2}{7}72​).
P9● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

A die has shown 1 or 2 on each of its last four throws. Tara says, "Numbers less than 3 are used up — they are less likely now." What is the probability of getting a number less than 3 on the next throw? Is Tara right?

Full solution

Given: a fair die; four earlier results. Asked: P(less than 3) on the next throw.

Concept used: theoretical probability counts the outcomes of this throw (Topic 2). Why it applies: a die has no memory.

  1. 1

    Next throw: 6 equally likely faces; less than 3: 1, 2.

  2. 2

    P=26=13P = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}P=62​=31​.

  3. 3

    Tara is wrong: the probability is 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​, the same as before every throw.

  4. Check: the die still has faces 1 to 6, so the counts (2 favourable out of 6) are the same as for the first throw ✔.

  5. Answer 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​; Tara is not right — earlier throws do not change it.

    Common trap: Thinking that a result that has "happened a lot" becomes less (or more) likely.

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P10●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

In a game, you throw a die once and win if it shows 4; otherwise you lose. Arun says, "I either win or lose, so P(win) =12= \dfrac{1}{2}=21​." Explain the mistake and find the correct P(win).

Full solution

Given: win only on 4. Asked: the mistake; P(win).

Concept used: the formula needs equally likely outcomes (Topic 2). Why it applies: "win" is 1 face and "lose" is 5 faces.

  1. 1

    The equally likely outcomes are the 6 faces, not "win" and "lose".

  2. 2

    Win: face 4 only → P(win)=16P(\text{win}) = \dfrac{1}{6}P(win)=61​.

  3. 3

    Lose: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 → 56\dfrac{5}{6}65​. "Win" and "lose" are not equally likely, so Arun's 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ is wrong.

  4. Check: 16+56=1\dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{5}{6} = 161​+65​=1 ✔.

  5. Answer Arun treats two unequal outcomes as equally likely. P(win)=16P(\text{win}) = \dfrac{1}{6}P(win)=61​.

    Common trap: Accepting "two outcomes, so 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​" without asking whether they are equally likely.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P11●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

All the hearts are removed from a deck of 52 cards. One card is drawn at random from the remaining cards. Find the probability that it is (a) a black card, (b) a red king.

Full solution

Given: 13 hearts removed (face cards are kings, queens and jacks; aces are not face cards). Asked: two probabilities.

Concept used: new total, new counts (Topic 4). Why it applies: the hearts cannot be drawn.

  1. 1

    Total: 52−13=3952 - 13 = 3952−13=39.

  2. 2

    (a) Black cards: all 26 are still there. P=2639=23P = \dfrac{26}{39} = \dfrac{2}{3}P=3926​=32​.

  3. 3

    (b) Red kings left: only the king of diamonds. P=139P = \dfrac{1}{39}P=391​.

  4. Check: the 39 cards are 26 black and 13 diamonds, and 2639+1339=1\dfrac{26}{39} + \dfrac{13}{39} = 13926​+3913​=1 ✔.

  5. Answer (a) 23\dfrac{2}{3}32​ (b) 139\dfrac{1}{39}391​

    Common trap: Keeping 52 as the total (12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ in (a)), or keeping 2 red kings in (b).

You got 0 of 2 parts.

P12●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

A box has 36 discs numbered 1 to 36. One disc is drawn at random. Find the probability that its number is (a) between 10 and 20, (b) a prime number less than 20.

Full solution

Given: 36 equally likely numbers. Asked: two probabilities.

Concept used: "between" leaves out the ends; 1 is not a prime (Topics 1, 4). Why it applies: both are counting traps.

  1. 1

    (a) Between 10 and 20: 11, 12, …, 19 → 9. P=936=14P = \dfrac{9}{36} = \dfrac{1}{4}P=369​=41​.

  2. 2

    (b) Primes less than 20: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 → 8. P=836=29P = \dfrac{8}{36} = \dfrac{2}{9}P=368​=92​.

  3. Check: (a) 19−11+1=919 - 11 + 1 = 919−11+1=9 ✔. (b) less than 20 leaves out 23, 29, 31 (the other primes up to 36) ✔.

  4. Answer (a) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ (b) 29\dfrac{2}{9}92​

    Common trap: Including 10 and 20 in (a) (1136\dfrac{11}{36}3611​), or 1 in (b).

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 2 parts.

P13●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Tickets numbered 1 to 80 are put in a box and one is drawn at random. Find the probability that the number on it is a perfect square or a perfect cube.

Full solution

Given: 80 equally likely numbers. Asked: P(square or cube).

Concept used: count A + count B − count of both (Topic 4). Why it applies: some numbers are both squares and cubes.

  1. 1

    Squares up to 80: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 → 8.

  2. 2

    Cubes up to 80: 1, 8, 27, 64 → 4.

  3. 3

    Both: 1 and 64 → 2.

  4. 4

    Favourable: 8+4−2=108 + 4 - 2 = 108+4−2=10. P=1080=18P = \dfrac{10}{80} = \dfrac{1}{8}P=8010​=81​.

  5. Check: list them: 1, 4, 8, 9, 16, 25, 27, 36, 49, 64 — 10 numbers ✔.

  6. Answer 18\dfrac{1}{8}81​

    Common trap: 8+4=128 + 4 = 128+4=12 counts 1 and 64 twice (320\dfrac{3}{20}203​).

P14●● StandardMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards (face cards are kings, queens and jacks; aces are not face cards). The probability that it is a red card or a face card is:

A + B − both (Topic 4). Why it applies: the 6 red face cards are in both groups.

26+1252=3852\dfrac{26 + 12}{52} = \dfrac{38}{52}5226+12​=5238​ counts the red face cards twice.
This takes the aces as face cards: 26+16−8=3426 + 16 - 8 = 3426+16−8=34.
This is "red and face" (6 cards).
3252=813\dfrac{32}{52} = \dfrac{8}{13}5232​=138​.

Given: 26 red cards, 12 face cards, 6 red face cards. Asked: P(red or face).

Concept used: A + B − both (Topic 4). Why it applies: the 6 red face cards are in both groups.

  1. 1

    26+12−6=3226 + 12 - 6 = 3226+12−6=32.

  2. 2

    P=3252=813P = \dfrac{32}{52} = \dfrac{8}{13}P=5232​=138​.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ 26+1252=3852\dfrac{26 + 12}{52} = \dfrac{38}{52}5226+12​=5238​ counts the red face cards twice.
    • (b) ✘ This takes the aces as face cards: 26+16−8=3426 + 16 - 8 = 3426+16−8=34.
    • (c) ✘ This is "red and face" (6 cards).
    • (d) ✔ 3252=813\dfrac{32}{52} = \dfrac{8}{13}5232​=138​.

  3. Check: the cards that are neither red nor face cards are the black non-face cards, 26−6=2026 - 6 = 2026−6=20, and 32+20=5232 + 20 = 5232+20=52 ✔.

  4. Answer (d)

    Common trap: Adding the two groups without taking away the overlap.
P15●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that the product of the two numbers is (a) at most 6, (b) more than 6.

Full solution

Given: 36 ordered pairs. Asked: two probabilities.

Concept used: at most 6 = 6 or less; the complement (Topics 3, 5). Why it applies: (b) is the opposite of (a).

  1. 1

    Products at most 6: first die 1 — any second (1 to 6): 6 pairs; first die 2 — second 1, 2, 3: 3 pairs; first die 3 — second 1, 2: 2 pairs; first die 4, 5, 6 — second 1: 3 pairs. Favourable: 6+3+2+3=146 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 146+3+2+3=14.

  2. 2

    (a) P=1436=718P = \dfrac{14}{36} = \dfrac{7}{18}P=3614​=187​.

  3. 3

    (b) P=1−718=1118P = 1 - \dfrac{7}{18} = \dfrac{11}{18}P=1−187​=1811​.

  4. Check: (b) directly — products more than 6: row 2 has 3 (4, 5, 6), row 3 has 4 (3 to 6), rows 4, 5, 6 have 5 each: 3+4+15=223 + 4 + 15 = 223+4+15=22, and 2236=1118\dfrac{22}{36} = \dfrac{11}{18}3622​=1811​ ✔.

  5. Answer (a) 718\dfrac{7}{18}187​ (b) 1118\dfrac{11}{18}1811​

    Common trap: Counting "less than 6" for "at most 6" — that leaves out (1, 6), (6, 1), (2, 3) and (3, 2).

P16●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Cards numbered 1 to 20 are shuffled and one is drawn. Find the probability that the number is (a) not a multiple of 3, (b) at least 15.

Full solution

Given: 20 equally likely numbers. Asked: two probabilities.

Concept used: complement; "at least" includes 15 (Topic 3). Why it applies: "not" is easier to count from its opposite.

  1. 1

    (a) Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 → 6. Not: 20−6=1420 - 6 = 1420−6=14. P=1420=710P = \dfrac{14}{20} = \dfrac{7}{10}P=2014​=107​.

  2. 2

    (b) At least 15: 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 → 6. P=620=310P = \dfrac{6}{20} = \dfrac{3}{10}P=206​=103​.

  3. Check: (a) P(multiple of 3)=620=310P(\text{multiple of 3}) = \dfrac{6}{20} = \dfrac{3}{10}P(multiple of 3)=206​=103​ and 710+310=1\dfrac{7}{10} + \dfrac{3}{10} = 1107​+103​=1 ✔.

  4. Answer (a) 710\dfrac{7}{10}107​ (b) 310\dfrac{3}{10}103​

    Common trap: In (b), counting 16 to 20 only ("more than 15") and getting 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 2 parts.

P17●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A coin is tossed three times. List all the outcomes. Find the probability that (a) heads and tails alternate, (b) the first two tosses are both heads, (c) the second and third tosses give the same result.

Full solution

Given: three tosses. Asked: the list and three probabilities.

Concept used: 8 ordered outcomes (Topic 5). Why it applies: each toss is equally likely to be H or T.

  1. 1

    HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT — 8.

  2. 2

    (a) Alternate: HTH, THT → 28=14\dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4}82​=41​.

  3. 3

    (b) First two heads: HHH, HHT → 28=14\dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4}82​=41​.

  4. 4

    (c) Second and third the same: HHH, HTT, THH, TTT → 48=12\dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{1}{2}84​=21​.

  5. Check: (c) count the other way: the second and third tosses differ in HHT, HTH, THT, TTH — 4 outcomes, and 4+4=84 + 4 = 84+4=8 ✔.

  6. Answer (a) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ (b) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ (c) 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​

    Common trap: In (b), writing only HHH — the third toss can be H or T.

You got 0 of 3 parts.

P18●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that (a) the two numbers differ by exactly 3, (b) one of the two numbers is a multiple of the other.

Full solution

Given: 36 ordered pairs. Asked: two probabilities.

Concept used: count both orders; a double counts once (Topic 5). Why it applies: (2, 4) and (4, 2) are different outcomes, but (3, 3) is one.

  1. 1

    (a) Difference 3: (1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6), (4, 1), (5, 2), (6, 3) → 6. P=636=16P = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}P=366​=61​.

  2. 2

    (b) Doubles (each number is a multiple of itself): 6. Other pairs where the larger is a multiple of the smaller: (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (1, 5), (1, 6), (2, 4), (2, 6), (3, 6) — 8, and their reverses — 8. Favourable: 6+8+8=226 + 8 + 8 = 226+8+8=22. P=2236=1118P = \dfrac{22}{36} = \dfrac{11}{18}P=3622​=1811​.

  3. Check: (b) count by the first die: 1 → 6 pairs; 2 → (2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 4), (2, 6): 4; 3 → (3, 1), (3, 3), (3, 6): 3; 4 → (4, 1), (4, 2), (4, 4): 3; 5 → (5, 1), (5, 5): 2; 6 → (6, 1), (6, 2), (6, 3), (6, 6): 4; 6+4+3+3+2+4=226 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 4 = 226+4+3+3+2+4=22 ✔.

  4. Answer (a) 16\dfrac{1}{6}61​ (b) 1118\dfrac{11}{18}1811​

    Common trap: In (b), counting each double twice (28 pairs), or forgetting the reverse pairs (14 pairs).

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ 1+0.31 + 0.31+0.3 — more than 1, so it cannot be a probability.
    • (b) ✔ 1−0.3=0.71 - 0.3 = 0.71−0.3=0.7.
    • (c) ✘ This is P(E)P(E)P(E) itself.
    • (d) ✘ 0.3−10.3 - 10.3−1 — negative, so it cannot be a probability.

  2. Check: 0.3+0.7=10.3 + 0.7 = 10.3+0.7=1 ✔.

  3. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Accepting an answer outside 0 to 1 — two of the options are impossible as probabilities.
P20●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

A leap year is chosen at random. Find the probability that it has 53 Fridays or 53 Saturdays.

Full solution

Given: 366 days. Asked: P(53 Fridays or 53 Saturdays).

Concept used: 366=52×7+2366 = 52 \times 7 + 2366=52×7+2; the 7 equally likely pairs of extra days (Topic 4). Why it applies: a 53rd Friday or Saturday comes from the extra days.

  1. 1

    Pairs: Sun–Mon, Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed, Wed–Thu, Thu–Fri, Fri–Sat, Sat–Sun.

  2. 2

    Pairs with a Friday or a Saturday: Thu–Fri, Fri–Sat, Sat–Sun → 3.

  3. 3

    P=37P = \dfrac{3}{7}P=73​.

  4. Check: P(53 Fridays) =27= \dfrac{2}{7}=72​ and P(53 Saturdays) =27= \dfrac{2}{7}=72​; the pair Fri–Sat gives both, so 27+27−17=37\dfrac{2}{7} + \dfrac{2}{7} - \dfrac{1}{7} = \dfrac{3}{7}72​+72​−71​=73​ ✔.

  5. Answer 37\dfrac{3}{7}73​

    Common trap: Adding 27+27=47\dfrac{2}{7} + \dfrac{2}{7} = \dfrac{4}{7}72​+72​=74​ — the pair Fri–Sat is counted twice.

P21●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AA fair coin is tossed four times and shows heads every time. The probability of a head on the fifth toss is 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​.
ROn every toss of a fair coin, heads and tails are equally likely, whatever the earlier tosses showed.
theoretical probability; a coin has no memory (Topic 2). Why it applies: the fifth toss has the same two equally likely outcomes.

Both true; R explains A.
R is the reason for A.
R is true.
A is true.

Given: four heads in a row. Asked: whether A and R are true, and whether R explains A.

Concept used: theoretical probability; a coin has no memory (Topic 2). Why it applies: the fifth toss has the same two equally likely outcomes.

  1. 1

    A: the fifth toss has outcomes H and T, equally likely: 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ — true.

  2. 2

    R: true for a fair coin — and it is exactly why A is true.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (A) ✔ Both true; R explains A.
    • (B) ✘ R is the reason for A.
    • (C) ✘ R is true.
    • (D) ✘ A is true.

  3. Check: if past tosses mattered, the answer would change with the history — but the coin, its faces and the toss are unchanged, so the count is still 1 favourable out of 2 ✔.

  4. Answer (A)

    Common trap: Thinking a tail is "due", which would make A false.
P22●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AWhen two dice are thrown, the probability that the sum is less than 5 is equal to the probability that the sum is more than 9.
RWhen two dice are thrown, each of the 11 possible sums 2, 3, …, 12 is equally likely.
the 36 ordered pairs are the equally likely outcomes, not the 11 sums (Topic 5). Why it applies: different sums have different numbers of pairs.

R is false.
R is false.
A is true; R is false.
A is true.

Given: two dice. Asked: whether A and R are true.

Concept used: the 36 ordered pairs are the equally likely outcomes, not the 11 sums (Topic 5). Why it applies: different sums have different numbers of pairs.

  1. 1

    A: sum less than 5 (2, 3, 4): 1+2+3=61 + 2 + 3 = 61+2+3=6 pairs; sum more than 9 (10, 11, 12): 3+2+1=63 + 2 + 1 = 63+2+1=6 pairs. Both 636=16\dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}366​=61​ — A is true.

  2. 2

    R: the sum 7 has 6 pairs but the sum 2 has only 1 — the sums are not equally likely, so R is false.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (A) ✘ R is false.
    • (B) ✘ R is false.
    • (C) ✔ A is true; R is false.
    • (D) ✘ A is true.

  3. Check: the grid is symmetric: the pair (a, b) has sum less than 5 exactly when (7 − a, 7 − b) has sum more than 9, so the two counts must be equal ✔.

  4. Answer (C)

    Common trap: Accepting R ("11 sums, so each is 111\dfrac{1}{11}111​") and then choosing (A) because A happens to be true.
P23●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that at least one of them shows an odd number.

Full solution

Given: 36 ordered pairs. Asked: P(at least one odd).

Concept used: at least one = 1 − none (Topics 3, 5). Why it applies: "none odd" means both even — one block of the grid.

  1. 1

    Both even: (2, 4, 6) × (2, 4, 6) → 3×3=93 \times 3 = 93×3=9. P(none odd)=936=14P(\text{none odd}) = \dfrac{9}{36} = \dfrac{1}{4}P(none odd)=369​=41​.

  2. 2

    P(at least one odd)=1−14=34P(\text{at least one odd}) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}P(at least one odd)=1−41​=43​.

  3. Check: count directly: first odd (any second) 3×6=183 \times 6 = 183×6=18; first even and second odd 3×3=93 \times 3 = 93×3=9; 18+9=2718 + 9 = 2718+9=27 and 2736=34\dfrac{27}{36} = \dfrac{3}{4}3627​=43​ ✔.

  4. Answer 34\dfrac{3}{4}43​

    Common trap: Finding "exactly one odd" (18 pairs, 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​) instead of "at least one".

  2. 2

    Red =14×36=9= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 36 = 9=41​×36=9; blue =13×36=12= \dfrac{1}{3} \times 36 = 12=31​×36=12.

  5. Answer 36 balls: 9 red, 12 blue (and 15 green).

P26●●● AdvancedLong answer · 5 marksOriginal

Priya and Kabir play a game with two dice. Priya wins a point if the sum of the numbers is a multiple of 4. Kabir wins a point if both numbers are prime. (If both happen, both win a point.) (a) Find the probability that Priya wins a point. (b) Find the probability that Kabir wins a point. (c) Is the game fair? (d) Find the probability that neither wins a point.

Full solution

Given: two dice, 36 ordered pairs. Asked: four answers.

Concept used: grid counting; A or B = A + B − both; complement (Topics 3–5). Why it applies: the two events overlap.

  1. 1

    (a) Sums 4, 8, 12: 3+5+1=93 + 5 + 1 = 93+5+1=9 pairs. P=936=14P = \dfrac{9}{36} = \dfrac{1}{4}P=369​=41​.

  2. 2

    (b) Primes on a die: 2, 3, 5. Both prime: 3×3=93 \times 3 = 93×3=9. P=936=14P = \dfrac{9}{36} = \dfrac{1}{4}P=369​=41​.

  3. 3

    (c) Yes — each has probability 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ of winning a point on a throw.

  4. 4

    (d) Both: both prime and sum a multiple of 4 — (2, 2) (sum 4), (3, 5), (5, 3) (sum 8) → 3. Priya or Kabir: 9+9−3=159 + 9 - 3 = 159+9−3=15. Neither: 36−15=2136 - 15 = 2136−15=21. P=2136=712P = \dfrac{21}{36} = \dfrac{7}{12}P=3621​=127​.

  5. Check: (d) list the 15 "someone wins" pairs: Priya's 9 — (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1), (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3), (6, 2), (6, 6); Kabir's that are not Priya's — (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 2), (3, 3), (5, 2), (5, 5) → 6; 9+6=159 + 6 = 159+6=15 ✔.

  6. Answer (a) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ (b) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ (c) Yes, the chances are equal. (d) 712\dfrac{7}{12}127​

    Common trap: In (d), 36−9−9=1836 - 9 - 9 = 1836−9−9=18 (12\dfrac{1}{2}21​) — the 3 pairs where both win were taken away twice.

P28●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A whole number is chosen at random from 1 to 120. Find the probability that it is divisible by 6 but not by 4.

Full solution

Given: 120 equally likely numbers. Asked: P(divisible by 6, not by 4).

Concept used: a number divisible by both 6 and 4 is a multiple of 12 (their LCM) (Topics 1, 4). Why it applies: take the multiples of 12 away from the multiples of 6.

    Favourable: 20−10=1020 - 10 = 1020−10=10. P=10120=112P = \dfrac{10}{120} = \dfrac{1}{12}P=12010​=121​.

  4. Check: the first few: 6, 18, 30, 42, … — every other multiple of 6 (the odd multiples of 6), so half of 20 = 10 ✔.

  5. Answer 112\dfrac{1}{12}121​

    Common trap: Taking away the multiples of 24 (6×46 \times 46×4) instead of 12: 20−5=1520 - 5 = 1520−5=15 and 18\dfrac{1}{8}81​.

P30●●● AdvancedLong answer · 5 marksOriginal

A box has 8 white balls and some black balls. If 4 more black balls are put into the box, the probability of drawing a black ball becomes 32\dfrac{3}{2}23​ times what it was before. Find the number of black balls in the box at first, and the two probabilities.

Full solution

Given: 8 white, x black; then x + 4 black. Asked: x and both probabilities.

Concept used: write each probability with x and form an equation (Topic 3; quadratic equations, Chapter 4). Why it applies: the totals are 8+x8 + x8+x and 12+x12 + x12+x.

  1. 1

    Before: P=x8+xP = \dfrac{x}{8 + x}P=8+xx​. After: P=x+412+xP = \dfrac{x + 4}{12 + x}P=12+xx+4​.

  2. 2

    x+412+x=32×x8+x\dfrac{x + 4}{12 + x} = \dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{x}{8 + x}12+xx+4​=23​×8+xx​.

  3. 3

    2(x+4)(8+x)=3x(12+x)2(x + 4)(8 + x) = 3x(12 + x)2(x+4)(8+x)=3x(12+x), so 2x2+24x+64=3x2+36x2x^2 + 24x + 64 = 3x^2 + 36x2x2+24x+64=3x2+36x.

  4. 4

    x2+12x−64=0x^2 + 12x - 64 = 0x2+12x−64=0, so (x+16)(x−4)=0(x + 16)(x - 4) = 0(x+16)(x−4)=0; x cannot be negative, so x=4x = 4x=4.

  5. 5

    Before: 412=13\dfrac{4}{12} = \dfrac{1}{3}124​=31​; after: 816=12\dfrac{8}{16} = \dfrac{1}{2}168​=21​.

  6. Check: 32×13=12\dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}23​×31​=21​ ✔.

  7. Answer 4 black balls at first; the probability goes from 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​ to 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​.

    Common trap: Adding the 4 balls to the black count but not to the total (writing x+48+x\dfrac{x + 4}{8 + x}8+xx+4​).

Given: three coins. Asked: what is wrong.

Concept used: 8 ordered outcomes (Topic 5). Why it applies: "no heads, 1 head, 2 heads, 3 heads" are not equally likely.

  1. 1

    Outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.

  2. 2

    No heads: only TTT → 18\dfrac{1}{8}81​, not 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​. One head: HTT, THT, TTH → 38\dfrac{3}{8}83​.

  3. Check: the four groups have 1, 3, 3, 1 outcomes — unequal, so they cannot each be 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ ✔.

  4. Answer The four results are not equally likely; P(no heads) =18= \dfrac{1}{8}=81​.

    Common trap: Using the number of heads as the outcomes.

E7● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 13, Ex 13.2 Q11

If you toss a coin 6 times and it comes down heads on each occasion. Can you say that the probability of getting a head is 1? Give reasons.

Full solution

Given: six heads in a row. Asked: is P(head) = 1?

Concept used: theoretical probability (Topic 2). Why it applies: each toss still has two equally likely outcomes.

  1. 1

    P(head) = 1 would mean a head is sure — but a tail is still possible on every toss.

  2. 2

    For a fair coin, P(head)=12P(\text{head}) = \dfrac{1}{2}P(head)=21​ on every toss, whatever happened before.

  3. Check: P(tail) would be 1−1=01 - 1 = 01−1=0, an impossible event — but the coin has a tail face that can land up ✔.

  4. Answer No. Heads and tails are equally likely on every toss, so P(head)=12P(\text{head}) = \dfrac{1}{2}P(head)=21​.

    Common trap: Using past results as the probability.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

E8● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 13, Ex 13.2 Q12

Sushma tosses a coin 3 times and gets tail each time. Do you think that the outcome of next toss will be a tail? Give reasons.

Full solution

Given: three tails. Asked: will the next toss be a tail?

Concept used: each toss is independent of the earlier ones (Topic 2). Why it applies: a coin has no memory.

  1. 1

    The next toss can be a head or a tail; they are equally likely.

  2. 2

    So we cannot say it will be a tail; P(tail)=12P(\text{tail}) = \dfrac{1}{2}P(tail)=21​.

  3. Check: P(head)=P(tail)=12P(\text{head}) = P(\text{tail}) = \dfrac{1}{2}P(head)=P(tail)=21​ — the same as on the first toss ✔.

  4. Answer No — it may be a head or a tail; each has probability 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​.

    Common trap: Predicting a "streak" will continue.

You got 0 of 1 parts.

E9● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 13, Ex 13.2 Q13

If I toss a coin 3 times and get head each time, should I expect a tail to have a higher chance in the 4th toss? Give reason in support of your answer.

Full solution

Given: three heads. Asked: is a tail more likely now?

Concept used: theoretical probability (Topic 2). Why it applies: the 4th toss has the same two equally likely outcomes.

  1. 1

    No — on the 4th toss, head and tail are still equally likely: P(tail)=12P(\text{tail}) = \dfrac{1}{2}P(tail)=21​.

  2. Check: nothing about the coin has changed, so the count (1 favourable of 2) is the same ✔.

  3. Answer No. Head and tail are equally likely on every toss.

    Common trap: Thinking a tail is "due" after several heads.

    Common trap: Using 310 as the number of "no prize" envelopes.

    (iii) One or two heads: 3+3=63 + 3 = 63+3=6 → 68=34\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}86​=43​.

  4. Check: 18+18+34=1\dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{3}{4} = 181​+81​+43​=1 ✔.

  5. Answer (i) 18\dfrac{1}{8}81​ (ii) 18\dfrac{1}{8}81​ (iii) 34\dfrac{3}{4}43​

    Common trap: Treating 0, 1, 2, 3 heads as equally likely (14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ each).

E49●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 13, Ex 13.3 Q39

A die has its six faces marked 0, 1, 1, 1, 6, 6. Two such dice are thrown together and the total score is recorded. (i) How many different scores are possible? (ii) What is the probability of getting a total of 7?

Full solution

Given: each die: 0, 1, 1, 1, 6, 6. Asked: the number of different scores; P(total 7).

Concept used: each face is one outcome (Topic 5). Why it applies: 1 is on three faces and 6 on two.

  1. 1

    (i) Each die shows 0, 1 or 6. Totals: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 2, 0 + 6 = 6, 1 + 6 = 7, 6 + 6 = 12 → 6 different scores: 0, 1, 2, 6, 7, 12.

  2. 2

    (ii) Total 7 = 1 on one die and 6 on the other: 3×2+2×3=123 \times 2 + 2 \times 3 = 123×2+2×3=12 face-pairs of 36 → 1236=13\dfrac{12}{36} = \dfrac{1}{3}3612​=31​.

  3. Check: (ii) the face-pairs by total: 0 — 1; 1 — 6; 2 — 9; 6 — 4; 7 — 12; 12 — 4; 1+6+9+4+12+4=361 + 6 + 9 + 4 + 12 + 4 = 361+6+9+4+12+4=36 ✔.

  4. Answer (i) 6 scores (0, 1, 2, 6, 7, 12) (ii) 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​

    Note on the official key: the Exemplar answer reads "5 scores (0, 1, 2, 6, 7, 12)", but the list it gives has six scores; 6 is correct.

    Common trap: In (ii), taking the faces as 0, 1, 6 only (9 outcomes) and getting 29\dfrac{2}{9}92​.

C1 — Case: a card game at home● FoundationCase/source-based · 4 marksCBSE Maths case bank, Probability, Case 1

(Picture, described: two hands holding playing cards over a table.)

On a weekend Rani was playing cards with her family .The deck has 52 cards.If her brother drew one card .

  1. Find the probability of getting a king of red colour.

a) 126\dfrac{1}{26}261​ b) 113\dfrac{1}{13}131​ c) 152\dfrac{1}{52}521​ d) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​

  1. Find the probability of getting a face card.

a) 126\dfrac{1}{26}261​ b) 113\dfrac{1}{13}131​ c) 213\dfrac{2}{13}132​ d) 313\dfrac{3}{13}133​

  1. Find the probability of getting a jack of hearts.

a) 126\dfrac{1}{26}261​ b) 152\dfrac{1}{52}521​ c) 352\dfrac{3}{52}523​ d) 326\dfrac{3}{26}263​

  1. Find the probability of getting a red face card.

a) 313\dfrac{3}{13}133​ b) 113\dfrac{1}{13}131​ c) 152\dfrac{1}{52}521​ d) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​

  1. Find the probability of getting a spade.

a) 126\dfrac{1}{26}261​ b) 113\dfrac{1}{13}131​ c) 152\dfrac{1}{52}521​ d) 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​

Full solution

Given: 52 well-shuffled cards; face cards are kings, queens and jacks (12); aces are not face cards. Asked: five probabilities.

Concept used: count on the 4 × 13 grid (Topic 4). Why it applies: each card is equally likely.

  1. 1

    Part 1: red kings 2 → 252=126\dfrac{2}{52} = \dfrac{1}{26}522​=261​ → a).

  2. 2

    Part 2: face cards 12 → 1252=313\dfrac{12}{52} = \dfrac{3}{13}5212​=133​ → d).

  3. 3

    Part 3: one card → 152\dfrac{1}{52}521​ → b).

  4. 4

    Part 4: red face cards 6 → 652=326\dfrac{6}{52} = \dfrac{3}{26}526​=263​ — not among the options.

  5. 5

    Part 5: spades 13 → 1352=14\dfrac{13}{52} = \dfrac{1}{4}5213​=41​ → d).

  6. Check: Part 4 is half of Part 2 (half of the face cards are red): 12×313=326\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{13} = \dfrac{3}{26}21​×133​=263​ ✔.

  7. Answer Part 1 a) · Part 2 d) · Part 3 b) 152\dfrac{1}{52}521​ · Part 4 326\dfrac{3}{26}263​ (none of the options) · Part 5 d)

    Note on the official key: the bank's key gives Part 3 as "b) 126\dfrac{1}{26}261​" — the letter b is right, but option b) is 152\dfrac{1}{52}521​, which is the correct value. It gives Part 4 as "a) 313\dfrac{3}{13}133​", which is the probability of any face card; a red face card is 652=326\dfrac{6}{52} = \dfrac{3}{26}526​=263​, which is not among the options. The parts repeat NCERT Exercise 14.1, Q14 (i)–(v).

    Common trap: Part 4 — choosing 313\dfrac{3}{13}133​ because it is the nearest option; always compute first.

C2 — Case: a board game with two dice● FoundationCase/source-based · 4 marksCBSE Maths case bank, Probability, Case 2

(Pictures, described: a "Business" board game and a pair of dice.)

Rahul and Ravi planned to play Business ( board game) in which they were supposed to use two dice.

  1. Ravi got first chance to roll the dice. What is the probability that he got the sum of the two numbers appearing on the top face of the dice is 8?

a) 126\dfrac{1}{26}261​ b) 536\dfrac{5}{36}365​ c) 118\dfrac{1}{18}181​ d) 0

  1. Rahul got next chance. What is the probability that he got the sum of the two numbers appearing on the top face of the dice is 13?

a) 1 b) 536\dfrac{5}{36}365​ c) 118\dfrac{1}{18}181​ d) 0

  1. Now it was Ravi's turn. He rolled the dice. What is the probability that he got the sum of the two numbers appearing on the top face of the dice is less than or equal to 12 ?

a) 1 b) 536\dfrac{5}{36}365​ c) 118\dfrac{1}{18}181​ d) 0

  1. Rahul got next chance. What is the probability that he got the sum of the two numbers appearing on the top face of the dice is equal to 7 ?

a) 59\dfrac{5}{9}95​ b) 536\dfrac{5}{36}365​ c) 16\dfrac{1}{6}61​ d) 0

  1. Now it was Ravi's turn. He rolled the dice. What is the probability that he got the sum of the two numbers appearing on the top face of the dice is greater than 8 ?

a) 1 b) 536\dfrac{5}{36}365​ c) 118\dfrac{1}{18}181​ d) 518\dfrac{5}{18}185​

Full solution

Given: two dice, 36 ordered pairs. Asked: five probabilities.

Concept used: the grid of sums (Topic 5). Why it applies: each pair is equally likely.

  1. 1

    Part 1: sum 8 — 5 pairs → 536\dfrac{5}{36}365​ → b).

  2. 2

    Part 2: sum 13 — impossible → 0 → d).

  3. 3

    Part 3: every sum is at most 12 → 1 (sure) → a).

  4. 4

    Part 4: sum 7 — 6 pairs → 636=16\dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}366​=61​ → c).

  5. 5

    Part 5: sums 9, 10, 11, 12: 4+3+2+1=104 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 104+3+2+1=10 → 1036=518\dfrac{10}{36} = \dfrac{5}{18}3610​=185​ → d).

  6. Check: Part 5's complement, sum at most 8, has 1+2+3+4+5+6+5=261 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 5 = 261+2+3+4+5+6+5=26 pairs, and 26+10=3626 + 10 = 3626+10=36 ✔.

  7. Answer Part 1 b) · Part 2 d) · Part 3 a) · Part 4 c) · Part 5 d)

    Note on the official key: the bank's key (1 b, 2 d, 3 a, 4 c, 5 d) is correct. Parts 1–3 repeat NCERT Example 13.

    Common trap: Part 5 — counting 8 as "greater than 8".
